issues.item: Fear of Rage: I will not be able to control my anger and will do something terrible
issues.explanation: The profile is centered on witnessed trauma with triggers involving crowded places, conversation topics, and bus riding, plus appraisals of vigilance and outsider status. The anger-loss-of-control appraisal introduces a distinct perpetration/impulse-control theme that is not supported by the other selected triggers, memory, threat, or strategy items, making it clinically hard to place within the same formulation.

Avoiding sex is not well linked to the rest of the profile. There are no sexual trauma cues, intimacy-related triggers, body-related appraisals, or threat/memory items that would explain sex-specific avoidance. Relative to the rest of the selected items, this strategy appears disconnected and inconsistent with the formulation.

vignette: At seventy-two, Catherine's life shifted when she witnessed a sudden outbreak of violence at a downtown bus depot. She had been waiting to board a route to her daughter's house when a heated argument near the turnstiles escalated into a physical altercation. A man was thrown against a metal support beam, the sharp crack of bone echoing over the sudden shrieks of the packed waiting crowd. Catherine froze, pressed shoulder-to-shoulder with strangers, watching the panic spread like a wave through the terminal. When she finally reached home, her hands trembled uncontrollably. The memory did not fade; it replayed with visceral clarity-the screech of the bus brakes, the specific cadence of the fight, the suffocating density of the crowd. In the months that followed, Catherine's daily reality narrowed as her triggers began to dictate her choices. She had come to believe the world was a dangerous place, a conviction that deepened every time she encountered a stimulus. Simply sitting on a bus, stepping into a crowded shopping center, or hearing neighbors debate sensitive crime-related conversation topics would instantly flood her with dread. Her constant vigilance did not merely warn her; it actively amplified her sensitivity to these stimuli, making every rumble of a transit vehicle or sudden shift in a crowd feel like a precursor to disaster. Because she felt permanently like an outsider to the life she once enjoyed, she began to interpret ordinary urban sounds as hostile threats that demanded immediate psychological armor. Fearing that she was powerless against future chaos, Catherine constructed rigid avoidance patterns and mental barriers. She avoided the event site entirely, routing herself miles out of her way to reach the grocery store, and refused to enter shopping centers or public events. When anxiety spiked during her daily network engineering work-often triggered by the rhythmic clack of her keyboard reminding her of the transit hub's chaos-she forced herself to think only positive thoughts, mentally cataloging safe memories of her garden or her husband's steady presence. Yet this relentless positive reframing and avoidance did not protect her; it starved her nervous system of corrective experiences, cementing her negative appraisals. By curating only safe, pleasant narratives and retreating from crowds, she reinforced her belief that she was permanently an outsider and that the world remained fundamentally unsafe. Worse, the cognitive strain of maintaining this fragile positivity made her more vulnerable to triggers the moment they breached her defenses. The cycle tightened across her professional and personal life. During a mandatory on-site security audit at a crowded technology conference center, the sheer density of the exhibition hall triggered a panic so severe she had to leave early, a decision that fractured her long-standing client relationships and forced her into a permanent remote role. Her husband noticed how she would quickly change the subject whenever conversation topics touched on public safety or sudden loss. She was certain that stepping back into the world would mean surrendering to the same terrifying chaos, yet her fear of isolation grew heavier. Now, Catherine sits in her quiet home office, the server racks humming softly behind her, wondering if she can learn to quiet the constant vigilance that has settled in her bones. She is hoping for a way to reclaim her independence and stop running, though she fears that any attempt to re-engage will only bring the crowds, the bus rides, and the conversations flooding back.
